title: PLC architecture
summary: What a programmable logic controller is made of: CPU, power supply, I/O modules, communication interfaces and the engineering software that programs it.

sections.heading: The controller in the cabinet
sections.body: A programmable logic controller (PLC) is an industrial computer built to control machines and processes. It reads **inputs** (buttons, sensors, transmitters), runs a **user program** and drives **outputs** (contactors, valves, lamps, drives). Compared with an office computer it is designed for a hostile environment: wide temperature ranges, electrical noise, vibration and years of continuous operation.

sections.heading: Main building blocks
sections.body:
- **CPU**: executes the program cyclically, holds the process images and the diagnostic buffer, and has a mode switch (RUN/STOP).
- **Power supply**: usually 24 V DC for the CPU and the I/O ("load" or "field" supply).
- **I/O modules**: convert field signals into data. Digital modules handle on/off signals, analog modules handle currents and voltages such as 4-20 mA.
- **Communication**: Ethernet ports for programming and fieldbuses (PROFINET, EtherNet/IP, EtherCAT, Modbus TCP) for remote I/O, drives and HMIs.
- **Rack or backplane**: holds the modules and gives each a **slot** number that the configuration refers to.

sections.heading: Configured versus installed hardware
sections.body: The engineer describes the hardware in the engineering software (the **hardware configuration**). The CPU compares this configuration with the modules really plugged in. A missing or wrong module is reported as a diagnostic event and the affected I/O delivers no valid values. PLC Lab models exactly this difference: the scene defines what is installed, the project defines what is configured.

sections.heading: Compact and modular controllers
sections.body: Compact controllers integrate CPU, some I/O and the power input in one housing and are expanded with side-mounted modules. Modular controllers use a rack or DIN-rail backplane with separate modules and usually offer more memory, more communication and redundancy options. Both execute the same kind of cyclic program.
